answer.summary: Early on, Chris Miller built products that served the institutional buyer more than the end user. The B2B2C setup kept his team distant from end users, making it hard to know whether a feature would win a contract or deliver real value to the person using it.

sections.heading: The mistake and what contributed
sections.content: In his first product-management job, Miller worked on a B2B2C product sold to institutions that white-labeled and resold it. Those institutional customers—not Miller’s team—owned the end-user relationship, leaving the team far from end users’ feedback. As a result, they built things to satisfy the buyer, not necessarily the person using the product; Miller said he likely shipped a lot of bad product during those years. He also described his early learning as painful trial and error, when there was little product-management content or access to people he could learn from.
